summary: The paper presents ExArch and ArTEMiS, two LLM-based approaches for traceability link recovery between software architecture documentation (SAD) and source code. ExArch extracts component names from SAD and/or code to generate simple software architecture models (SAMs) for transitive linking via TransArC. ArTEMiS uses LLMs for architectural entity recognition and matching to establish SAD-to-SAM trace links. Evaluated on a benchmark of five open-source projects, comparing against multiple baselines with various LLMs, using precision, recall, and F1-score metrics and statistical tests.

summary: This study evaluates three LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, o3-mini) for documentation-to-code traceability using two novel datasets (Unity Catalog and Crawl4AI). summary: DDD-Enforcer is a VS Code extension that enforces Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles through real-time analysis combining AST inspection with Large Language Models (LLMs). title: Exploring LLMs for Verifying Technical System Specifications Against Requirements
venue: 2024 IEEE 3rd Industrial Electronics Society Annual On-Line Conference (ONCON)
QA1_rationale: The research question is explicitly stated: 'Can LLMs perform inferences comparable to those of conventional rule-based systems in determining which requirements from a given list of requirements are fulfilled by a given system specification?'
QA2_rationale: Methods are described in detail: experimental context, creation of dataset via SysML and OCL to establish ground truth, metrics (precision, recall, f1), experimental variables, and evaluation procedure. The process is clear enough to replicate the general approach.
QA3_rationale: The dataset is explicitly described: synthetic, smart-grid domain, system specifications as workflows with varying complexities, requirements as constraints. The paper states 27 unique combinations of specifications and requirement sets, with 1944 total evaluations. Origin, size, and context are clearly reported.
QA4_rationale: Evaluation uses a ground truth derived from formal SysML/OCL models, and LLM outputs are compared with precision, recall, and f1-score. This design directly matches the research question of comparing LLM inferences to rule-based systems.
QA5_rationale: Model versions and prompting strategies are named, but the exact prompt texts, temperature, and other settings are not provided in the paper. A GitHub repository is referenced for materials, but the paper alone lacks full configuration details.
QA6_rationale: Results are reported as averages in Table I and discussed qualitatively. However, no statistical measures (e.g., confidence intervals, standard deviations) or deeper error analysis are provided, limiting the depth of the analysis.
QA7_rationale: Conclusions are directly backed by the results, with clear recommendations. Limitations are candidly discussed, including the small synthetic dataset and untested LLMs like GPT-o1.
QA8_rationale: All experimental materials (code, data, prompts, SysML models, OCL constraints) are made publicly available on GitHub. Funding sources are declared, and no conflicts of interest are apparent.
summary: The study experimentally investigates whether LLMs can verify technical system specifications against requirements, comparing their inferences to a formal rule-based benchmark using SysML and OCL. It varies system specification complexity, number of non-fulfilled requirements, number of requirements, prompting strategy, LLM architecture, and textual style across 1944 evaluations in a smart-grid domain. Results report f1-scores per variable for four LLMs, with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieving the best performance but still falling short of formal methods.
